verified_facts.fact: Anthropic's own newsroom dates this piece 2026-09-17 and gives it this summary, which is also the clearest one-sentence statement of what was announced.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Today, the world can’t see what’s going on inside AI labs. Anthropic is proposing new metrics that would give the public visibility into frontier AI development.

verified_facts.fact: What was published: three measurements intended to let the public track AI development inside frontier labs - how much AI R&D is performed by AI itself, how well AI agents' actions are overseen, and how compute is allocated.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: To do that, we’re sharing three measurements that will help the public track AI development inside frontier AI labs

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic frames the reason in one sentence at the top of the piece.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: AI systems are getting more powerful, and they’re increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic states that it plans to embed independent third-party evaluators from multiple organizations, with access comparable to internal risk assessment teams, to verify safety practices, report incidents and monitor metrics like these. This is a plan, not something already in place.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: We plan to embed independent third-party evaluators from multiple organizations at Anthropic, and give them access to internal processes, systems, and data comparable to what internal risk assessment teams have.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic says the numbers themselves would be expected to move if labs coordinated on pacing, and ties that explicitly to its CEO's call.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: It’s important to note that we would expect these numbers to shift if there were coordination on pacing the frontier, as called for by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

verified_facts.fact: Measurement 1 is called the Anthropic R&D Automation Index, and Anthropic describes it as a prototype built by cataloguing the kinds of AI R&D work at the company, rating how automated each is, and aggregating the ratings.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: We built a prototype index of how much of Anthropic’s AI research and development (R&D) is performed by Claude, called the Anthropic R&D Automation Index.

verified_facts.fact: The rating scale is not Anthropic's own: it is an Automation Level (AL) scale developed by Epoch AI running from AL0 to AL5. At AL3 AI 'collaborates' - large chunks of work under close human direction. At AL4 AI 'leads' - most of the task end-to-end from a high-level prompt, with the human supervising.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: we use an automation rating scale developed by Epoch AI that measures “Automation Level,” or AL. It runs from AL0 (no AI involvement) to AL5 (AI operates fully autonomously, with no human in the loop).

verified_facts.fact: The three headline results of measurement 1, all stated 'As of August 2026': Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work; Claude 'leads' 26% of Anthropic's AI R&D work; and the share of work at or above 'AI collaborates' is above 90%.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work. Claude “leads” 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D work. The share of work at or above “AI collaborates” is above 90%.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic names two obstacles to comparing labs: no common methodology, and the fact that it is using its own models to evaluate its own systems, so the judge model could repeat the errors of the model it is checking.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Second, we’re using our own models to evaluate our systems, which could mean that the “judge” model could make the same kinds of errors as the model it is checking.

verified_facts.fact: Measurement 2 covers three oversight metrics, defined by Anthropic as coverage (share of an agent's actions passing through a monitor), review latency (time between an action and its review) and escalation rate (share blocked, redirected or flagged).
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: we consider three different metrics: coverage, which describes the share of an agent’s actions that pass through a monitor before or after execution; review latency , which is the time between an action and its review, first by an automated monitor and then by a human; and escalation rate, which is the share of agent activities that are either blocked/redirected (in the case of online monitors) or flagged for further review (in the case of offline monitors).

verified_facts.fact: Scale, with its scope limit attached: as of August 2026 roughly 30,000 agents were doing research and engineering work at Anthropic at any one time on its most-used internal platform, and Anthropic says the measurements cover that platform only.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: As of August 2026, there were approximately 30,000 agents doing research and engineering work at Anthropic at any one time in our most-used internal platform. These measurements cover this platform only.

verified_facts.fact: Online monitors check actions in real time and either block dangerous actions or steer misbehaviour automatically; Anthropic's stated example of what they are for is an agent copying model weights out of its systems.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: They’re built to address harms that would happen quickly and could not be undone, such as an agent copying model weights out of our systems.

verified_facts.fact: Coverage figures: Anthropic states 100% of these agents' actions pass through the online monitor before execution, usually within seconds, and 100% are ingested by the offline monitor after they are taken.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: 100% of these agents’ actions pass through the online monitor before they are executed, usually within seconds.

verified_facts.fact: Review latency: automated review happens before the action; humans review any blocked actions within one week. The offline monitor flags roughly 100,000 transcripts per week, most of which are resolved by classifiers, with approximately ~50 per week escalated to human review.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The monitor flags roughly 100,000 transcripts per week that are then reviewed by multiple classifiers for false-positives and initial oversight review. Most of the flags are resolved by this process, and the highest priority flags (approximately ~50 per week) are escalated to human review.

verified_facts.fact: Blocking rate, with its exact denominator and window: Anthropic says it analysed over a billion decisions from its research and engineering agents over August 2026 and found 0.002% of them - about 1 in 47,000 - were blocked by the online monitor. Separately, the offline monitor flags roughly one to two transcripts in every thousand for further review.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: We analyzed over a billion decisions from our research & engineering agents over August 2026 and found that 0.002% of them (about 1 in 47,000) were blocked by this monitor.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic's own caveat about rare events at scale, which is the sentence that makes the 0.002% figure meaningful rather than reassuring.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: In our monitoring data to date, individual agents rarely misbehave. But when there are millions or billions of agents operating in the economy, even rare events can happen regularly.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic states that METR has independently red-teamed its offline monitoring platform in the past.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: In the past, METR has independently red-teamed our offline monitoring platform .

verified_facts.fact: Measurement 3 is a compute snapshot covering one week, 13 to 20 July 2026, in which every workload was sorted into categories and the safety share of AI R&D compute was calculated.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: We examined a snapshot of how Anthropic used all of its compute from July 13 to July 20

verified_facts.fact: The two compute results, which must always be written as a pair because they have different denominators: about 6% of compute that went to AI R&D went to safety, and about 12% of compute that went to AI-driven AI R&D went to safety.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Over the examined week, about 6% of compute that went to AI R&D was allocated toward safety, and about 12% of compute that went to AI-driven AI R&D was allocated toward safety.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic labels those two figures deliberately conservative and explains one rule that makes them so: a token that advanced capabilities as much as safety was not counted. It also says the figures exclude safeguards classifiers, which it describes as a separate, comparable amount of compute.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: These are deliberately conservative estimates. For example, if a token was used to advance capabilities as much as it was to advance safety, it was not counted in these metrics.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic states plainly that compute is an imperfect proxy for how much a company focuses on safety, because safety research is researcher-time-intensive rather than compute-intensive, and says the value of the metric is comparison over time rather than the absolute numbers.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Safety research tends to use less compute than frontier training runs by its nature, so compute is an imperfect proxy for how much a company focuses on safety.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic anticipates the obvious objection to a self-reported safety share and says where the burden of proof should sit.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Safety research is hard to distinguish from capabilities research, and each developer will be tempted to draw the line generously. The burden of proof should sit with the developer to show that work is safety-related.

verified_facts.fact: Methodology for the automation index, published in the appendix: for each week in July 2026 Anthropic randomly sampled 20% of staff from each department in the model R&D loop, had a Claude research agent list that person's tasks from Slack and internal documentation, and built a flat list of roughly 15,000 granular model R&D tasks.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: For each week in July 2026, we randomly sampled 20% of staff from each department that make up the model R&D loop.

verified_facts.fact: Those tasks were organised by Claude into a frozen hierarchical tree of 542 nodes, of which 378 are leaves, with examples named such as 'eval platform defect diagnosis and fixes'.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The resulting tree has 542 nodes at different depths, of which 378 are leaves like “eval platform defect diagnosis and fixes,” “RL sandbox egress and network policy,” and “serving incident postmortems.”

verified_facts.fact: The rating is done by Claude too: a Claude agent researches each node and an independent Claude judge assigns one of six automation levels, seeing only evidence from the rated month or earlier.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: When we rate a given month’s automation, we only allow the research agents that do the ratings to see evidence from that month or earlier.

verified_facts.fact: Weighting is by person-time rather than by editorial judgement of importance.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Rather than deciding ourselves what kinds of work are more important than others, we used the amount of person-time dedicated to that task as a proxy.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic states in a footnote that AL5 is a level it has not yet reached, and describes what it would look like: the model would monitor for failures itself, scope the investigation, design, implement, test and deploy the fix, with no human involved unless one wanted to be.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: a level we have not yet reached

verified_facts.fact: A second footnote limits the compute figure further: Anthropic manages compute as a single fungible pool directed dynamically, so the week is a snapshot of where capacity happened to go, not a fixed allocation, and the categories do not correspond to how expenses are classified.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: so this is a snapshot of how capacity happened to be directed in one week, not a fixed allocation

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic's closing statement of purpose, which is the piece's thesis in one line.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: As the world considers pacing the frontier, we should do everything possible to minimize the gap between what frontier labs know and what the public knows.

verified_facts.fact: The Advanced AI Framework (AAIF) that the piece refers to is a published Anthropic policy proposal, described on Anthropic's policy page as covering transparency, independent evaluation, and government authority to block or deter dangerous deployments. It is a proposal to governments, not an existing rule.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: The first, our Advanced AI Framework, offers a roadmap for governing increasingly capable systems, from transparency and independent evaluation to government authority to block or deter dangerous deployments.

verified_facts.fact: Anthropic's policy page states the framing behind both proposals.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: AI is advancing at exponential speed, and the policymaking process was built for a slower world.

not_said: NO REGION, PRODUCT OR USER IMPACT. This is a transparency proposal about how Anthropic builds models. As checked to 2026-09-18, the page names no country, no market, no product change and no user-facing feature. Nothing here changes what a Claude user in Taiwan can do, and the article must not suggest otherwise.

No other lab's numbers. Anthropic publishes only its own figures and says any frontier developer 'could' publish the same measures. As checked on the page to 2026-09-18, no other company's automation share, oversight coverage or safety compute share appears. The article must not present 26% or 6%/12% as an industry figure or imply anyone else is higher or lower.

No commitment to a publication schedule. Anthropic says it hopes to model transparency and 'will continue to do so', and that any developer 'could publish these measures regularly'. It does not commit to a cadence, a next publication date, or a fixed methodology.

No third-party verification of any figure published here. Anthropic says it plans to embed independent evaluators and that METR has red-teamed its offline monitoring platform in the past; it does not say any outside party has checked the 26%, the 30,000 agents, the 0.002%, or the 6%/12%.
No absolute compute figures. The compute section publishes only shares of AI R&D compute. No chip count, no spend, no total.
No headcount and no cost. The automation index is weighted by person-time but no staff number is published, and the piece says nothing about jobs at Anthropic.

No definition of 'safety work' that anyone outside Anthropic can apply. Anthropic says category definitions should be published alongside and checked by an independent third party, and that developers should converge on a shared definition ahead of time - which means there is not one yet.

No scope beyond one internal platform for the oversight numbers. Anthropic states the agent measurements cover its most-used internal platform only, and says nothing about agents running elsewhere in the company or in customer deployments.

No claim that recursive self-improvement is close or inevitable on this page. It defines the term and says the measurement exists to understand how close the world is to it. The article must not add a timeline.
No response from any other lab, and no reference to OpenAI's misalignment reporting framework published the previous day. Anthropic names no competitor anywhere in the piece.

editorial_brief:
READER AND ANGLE. Written for a Taiwanese general reader who followed the 9/12 story about Anthropic's CEO calling for the frontier to be slowed down and asked the obvious next question: slowed down from what, measured how, and who would check? This piece is the answer one company gave five days later, and it is unusual because it is a company publishing numbers about itself that nobody can currently audit. The spine is therefore not 'AI is building AI' - that headline is available anywhere - but 'what does a measurable claim about a lab look like, and what would it take for the public to trust one'.

THE CENTRAL FACT TO GET RIGHT. 26% is 'Claude leads', which on Epoch AI's scale means the human still supervises; Anthropic states that fully autonomous has not been reached for any measured subset. Every published figure is also bound to a window - August 2026 for automation and oversight, 13-20 July for compute - and to a scope, in the oversight case a single internal platform. A reviewer will check the 26% framing first and the windows second.

WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A READER'S TIME. The three numbers each carry their own visible weakness, and Anthropic printed the weaknesses itself: the automation index is rated by Claude judging Claude; the oversight figures cover one platform; the compute share admits that safety research is not compute-hungry so the proxy is poor. That is the actual story - a first attempt at a public yardstick, published with its own caveats attached, by the only party who can currently read the underlying data. The reader's takeaway is a way to read any future 'AI safety' number: ask the window, the denominator, the scope and who checked.

SUGGESTED FIVE SECTIONS. (1) What Anthropic published on 2026-09-17 and why it says it did, including that it expects the numbers to move if labs coordinate. (2) The three measurements in plain language, ending with the required table (max 4 columns: 指標 / 期間 / 官方數字 / 官方自己標的限制; 3-4 rows; caption dated 2026-09-18). (3) Why a self-reported number is not yet a verified one: Claude judging Claude, one internal platform, 'we plan to embed' evaluators, METR in the past tense; diagram goes here. (4) The two numbers most likely to be misread - 26% 'leads' versus autonomous, and 0.002% blocked versus 'rare events happen regularly at scale'. (5) What Anthropic did not say, and how this connects to the 9/12 essay without restating it.

ORIGINAL SCENARIO, to be labelled as an editorial example per BRIEF. A reader sees a company report that '99.9% of requests passed a safety check'. The editorial point is that the sentence is unreadable until you know the window, the denominator, the scope and who verified it - the same four questions this piece hands you, applied to a claim the reader will actually meet in a product page or a press release.

TONE AND SCOPE. Plain, neither credulous nor cynical; Anthropic is grading itself and saying so. Deliberately out of scope: any comparison with OpenAI or any other lab (Anthropic makes none); any timeline for recursive self-improvement; any restatement of the 9/12 three-step plan; any material from the risk-report PDF or the undated 'When AI builds itself' page; any claim about Claude users in Taiwan, since this announcement changes nothing for them.

Every string must also appear in the body, and no numeral appears in the diagram.
